q: What is data privacy?
r: Protecting personal information from being misused or seen by the wrong people
Individuals should control how their data is used.
w: Making data as large as possible
Keeping data in a locked room only
Physical locks are only one part.

q: What is personally identifiable information (PII)?
r: Information that can identify a specific person
Names and Social Security numbers are examples.
w: Information that is true for everyone
Information that is encrypted by default
Information that is deleted after use

q: Which of these is PII?
r: A person's home address and phone number
It points to one individual.
w: The number of days in a week

q: What is anonymization of data?
r: Removing or hiding details that identify individuals
The data can then be shared more safely.
w: Adding a person's name to every record
Copying data to a public site

q: Why can supposedly anonymous data still identify people?
r: Combining details such as birth date, zip code and gender can single someone out
Linking data sets can re-identify individuals.
w: That is not how it works.

q: What is informed consent in data collection?
r: People understand how their data will be used and agree to it
Clear explanations come first.
w: People are tricked into sharing data
Data is collected without telling anyone
People are required to share all data

q: What is the principle of data minimization?
r: Collect only the data you actually need
Less data means less risk.
w: Collect as much data as possible
Delete data after the first use only

q: What is a data breach?
r: An incident in which private data is accessed or exposed without permission
It can harm people and companies.
w: A planned backup of the data

q: A company discovers hackers stole customer emails. What should it do first?
r: Contain the breach and notify affected people as required
Quick action limits harm.
w: Hiding it increases harm and may break laws.
That does not solve the problem.

q: What is encryption?
r: Scrambling data so only authorized people can read it
It protects data in storage and transit.
w: Making data easier for everyone to read

q: What is multi-factor authentication?
r: Requiring two or more ways to prove identity before access
A password plus a code is an example.
w: Using one very long password only
Sharing a password with a team
Writing a password on a note

q: What does GDPR protect?
r: Personal data of people in the European Union
It gives people rights over their data.
w: The prices of goods in Europe

q: What does CCPA give California residents?
r: Rights to know about, delete and opt out of the sale of their personal data
It is a state privacy law.
w: A right to avoid all taxes
A right to see anyone's data

q: What does COPPA protect?
r: Online privacy of children under 13
Sites need parental consent to collect their data.

q: What does HIPAA protect?
r: The privacy and security of health information
Healthcare providers must follow it.

q: What does FERPA protect?
r: The privacy of student education records
Schools need permission to share them.

q: What is AI ethics?
r: Principles about developing and using AI in fair, safe and responsible ways
It addresses harm, bias and accountability.
w: Rules that make AI run faster
A method for storing AI models

q: What is algorithmic bias?
r: Unfair outcomes from an algorithm that favors or harms certain groups
Biased data can cause it.
w: An algorithm that runs very quickly
An algorithm with no input data

q: A loan model approves fewer applicants from one neighborhood even when finances are equal. What is the likely issue?
r: Algorithmic bias
The model treats similar people unfairly.

q: Which step best reduces bias in an AI system?
r: Using diverse, representative data and testing results across groups
Checking outcomes reveals unfair patterns.
w: Training on data from one group only

q: What is transparency in AI?
r: Being open about how a system works and makes decisions
People can understand and question results.

q: What is explainable AI?
r: AI whose decisions can be understood by people
It helps build trust and find errors.
w: AI that refuses to answer questions
AI that is hidden from users

q: What is accountability in AI?
r: Clear responsibility for the outcomes an AI system causes
Someone must answer for harm.
w: Blaming the computer for every error
Counting the money spent on AI

q: An AI tool wrongly denies a customer's claim. Who should be accountable?
r: The organization that deployed the tool
People remain responsible for automated decisions.
w: No one, because it was automated
The customer who made the claim

q: What is a deepfake?
r: Fake media created by AI that makes someone appear to say or do something
It can spread false information.

q: Why are deepfakes an ethical concern?
r: They can deceive people and damage reputations
Trust in media can be harmed.

q: What is copyright concern with AI training data?
r: Whether creators' work was used without permission
Courts and lawmakers are working on the issue.
w: Whether the computer is the correct size
Whether the data is too clean
Whether the model is named correctly

q: Which practice respects creators when using AI-generated content?
r: Checking permissions and giving proper credit where required
Responsible use respects rights.
w: Copying any work found online as your own

q: What is human oversight in AI?
r: People reviewing and being able to override AI decisions
It helps catch mistakes.
w: Letting the AI run with no review

q: Which decision is most appropriate to keep under human review rather than fully automating?
r: Denying a person's medical treatment
Serious decisions need human judgment.

q: What is surveillance concern with AI?
r: Tracking people's activities in ways that can invade privacy
Face recognition is a common example.

q: A store uses face recognition on every shopper without telling them. What is the main concern?
r: It may invade privacy without consent
People did not agree to the tracking.
w: It lowers the price of goods

q: What is data ownership?
r: Who has rights to control and use a set of data
Rules vary by law and agreement.
w: Who stores the data on a shelf

q: What is a privacy policy?
r: A statement explaining how an organization collects, uses and protects data
Users should read it before sharing information.
w: A rule that blocks all websites

q: Before signing up for an app, what should a user check about their data?
r: What data is collected and how it is shared
This shows the privacy trade-off.
w: Only the color of the app icon
That is not about data use.
Nothing, since all apps are identical

q: What is phishing?
r: A scam that tricks people into giving away sensitive information
It often uses fake emails or links.
w: That is not the tech meaning.

q: An email from 'IT' asks you to enter your password on a strange link. What should you do?
r: Not click and report the email
It is likely phishing.

q: What is the principle of fairness in AI?
r: Systems should treat people equitably and avoid discrimination
Outcomes should not harm certain groups.
w: Systems should hide how they work
Systems should always be the cheapest

q: Which is the best reason to audit an AI system regularly?
r: To find errors, bias or harmful outcomes that appear over time
Ongoing checks protect users.
w: To make the system more expensive
To remove the need for rules
To keep users from seeing results

q: What is responsible AI?
r: Building and using AI that is safe, fair and accountable
It considers impact on people and society.
w: Building AI as fast as possible without testing
Using AI only to cut costs

q: What does it mean to be data literate?
r: Being able to read, understand and question data and its conclusions
It includes spotting misleading charts.
w: Being able to memorize large tables
Being able to type very fast
Being able to buy data cheaply

q: A bar chart starts its vertical axis at 90 instead of 0 to exaggerate a small difference. What is this?
r: A misleading visualization
The scale makes differences look larger.
w: It changes how data looks, not the data.
It is not a privacy method.

q: What is a data-driven decision?
r: A choice based on analysis of data rather than guesswork
Evidence supports the decision.
w: A choice made by flipping a coin
A choice made by the loudest voice
A choice made without any information

q: A manager sees that sales rose after a new ad and says the ad caused the rise. What should an analyst check?
r: Whether other factors, such as seasons or promotions, could explain it
Correlation is not proof of cause.
w: Only the color of the ad
